content: Many severe diseases are classified under the category of zoonoses. The term zoonosis originates from the Greek words zoon, meaning animal (IPA: zo'o̞n), and nosos, meaning disease. The plural form of zoonosis is zoonoses, and an alternative singular form is zoonose. A zoonosis is defined as a disease that can be transmitted from animals to humans. A more technical definition describes it as a disease that primarily exists in animals but can also infect humans. The interdisciplinary field of conservation medicine, which combines human and veterinary medicine with environmental sciences, focuses significantly on zoonotic diseases. Carriers of Zoonotic Diseases A variety of animals can act as carriers of infectious organisms that may cause zoonotic diseases. These include bats, birds, cats, cattle, chimpanzees, dogs, fish, fleas, geese, goats, horses, humans, monkeys, mosquitoes, opossums, pigs, rabbits, raccoons, rats, rodents, snails, sloths, and sheep. Infectious Agents of Zoonoses Zoonotic diseases can be caused by various infectious agents, including: Parasites (e.g., protozoa, helminths, cestodes, trematodes) Bacteria Viruses Fungi Prions Examples of Important Zoonotic Diseases Some of the most significant zoonotic diseases include: Anthrax Avian Influenza (Bird Flu) Bolivian Hemorrhagic Fever Brucellosis Borrelia infections Bornavirus infection Bubonic Plague Campylobacteriosis Chagas Disease Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (vCJD), a transmissible spongiform encephalopathy (TSE) linked to Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE or Mad Cow Disease) Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Cutaneous Larval Migrans Dengue Fever Ebola Fever Echinococcosis Hantavirus infections Korean Hemorrhagic Fever Lassa Fever Leishmaniasis Leptospirosis Listeriosis Marburg Virus Infection Monkey B Virus Nipah Virus Ocular Larval Migrans Ornithosis (Psittacosis) Oropouche Fever Q Fever Psittacosis (Parrot Fever) Plague Rabies Rift Valley Fever Ringworm (e.g., Tinea canis) Salmonellosis Sodoku Toxoplasmosis Trichinosis Typhus and other Rickettsial diseases Venezuelan Hemorrhagic Fever Visceral Larval Migrans Yellow Fever Other zoonotic diseases include Glanders and potentially SARS, which may involve civet cats as either a source of infection or as secondary victims of human transmission. This list is not exhaustive. Influenza Virus as a Zoonotic Example The influenza virus is a notable example of a zoonotic pathogen. It frequently recombines genetic material between strains found in humans, swine, and avian species, leading to the emergence of new strains with altered characteristics. Occasionally, such as during the 1918 pandemic, these new strains can result in catastrophic global mortality. Historical Development of Zoonotic Diseases During most of human prehistory, populations consisted of small, isolated bands of hunter-gatherers, typically fewer than 150 individuals. These groups rarely interacted with others, which limited the spread of epidemic or pandemic diseases. Such diseases, which require a continuous influx of susceptible hosts, often burned out after their initial spread through a population. For a pathogen to persist, it needed to establish chronic infections, remain viable in a host for extended periods, or have a non-human reservoir to survive between human hosts. In many cases, humans are accidental hosts and represent a dead-end for the pathogen. Examples include rabies, anthrax, tularemia, and West Nile virus. Consequently, much of human development has been shaped by zoonotic diseases rather than epidemic diseases. Many modern diseases, including epidemic ones, originated as zoonotic infections. Evidence suggests that diseases such as measles, smallpox, influenza, and diphtheria were initially transmitted to humans from animals. HIV, the common cold, and tuberculosis may also have zoonotic origins. Modern Relevance of Zoonoses Zoonotic diseases are of significant concern today because they often represent previously unrecognized illnesses or exhibit increased virulence in populations lacking immunity. For example, the West Nile virus emerged in the United States in 1999, spreading across the country by 2002 and causing widespread distress. Other zoonotic diseases include bubonic plague, salmonella, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and Lyme disease. Zoonotic outbreaks can result from human encroachment into wilderness areas or the movement of wild animals into human-inhabited regions due to anthropogenic or environmental disturbances. For instance, the 1999 Nipah virus outbreak in peninsular Malaysia occurred when intensive pig farming encroached on the natural habitat of fruit bats carrying the virus. Similarly, avian influenza and West Nile virus have recently spilled over into human populations, likely due to interactions between carrier hosts and domestic animals. Highly mobile animals, such as bats and birds, pose a greater risk of zoonotic transmission due to their ability to move easily into human habitats. Diseases like malaria, schistosomiasis, river blindness, and elephantiasis, while transmitted by insects or involving intermediate host vectors, are not considered zoonotic because they rely on humans for part of their life cycle. Zoonotic Outbreaks Linked to Fairs and Petting Zoos Zoonotic outbreaks have been associated with human-animal interactions at fairs, petting zoos, and similar settings. In 2005, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued updated recommendations to prevent zoonotic transmission in public settings. These guidelines, developed with the National Association of State Public Health Veterinarians, addressed educational responsibilities of venue operators, management of public-animal contact, and animal care practices. Notable Outbreaks In 1988, a person contracted and died from Swine Influenza Virus (Swine Flu) after visiting a pig barn at a Wisconsin county fair. Three healthcare workers treating the patient also developed flu-like symptoms, with laboratory evidence confirming Swine Flu infection. The CDC concluded that the virus was transmitted directly from pigs to humans. In 1994, seven cases of E. coli O157:H7 infection were traced to a farm in Leicestershire, UK. Epidemiological investigations revealed that the strain isolated from nine animals on the farm was identical to the strain found in human samples, implicating direct human-animal contact as the source. In 1995, 43 children in Wales became ill with cryptosporidiosis after visiting a rural farm. Cryptosporidium was isolated from seven of the children, and investigations linked the illness to contact with calves. A similar outbreak occurred in Dublin, Ireland, where 13 children contracted cryptosporidiosis after visiting a farm. A case-control study associated the illness with playing in a sand area near a stream accessible to animals. In 1997, an E. coli O157:H7 outbreak was identified among three children who had visited an open farm. Two of the children developed hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Isolates from the children and farm samples were identical, confirming the link. In 1999, the largest waterborne E. coli O157:H7 outbreak in U.S. history occurred at the Washington County Fair in New York. Investigations linked the outbreak to beverages made with water from an unchlorinated fairground well. A total of 127 cases were confirmed, with 71 hospitalizations, 14 cases of HUS, and two deaths. In 2000, 51 people became ill with E. coli O157:H7 infections after visiting a Pennsylvania dairy farm. Eight children developed HUS. Investigations attributed the outbreak to contamination on animal hides and in the environment. Also in 2000, 43 visitors to the Medina County Fair in Ohio contracted E. coli O157:H7 infections. The outbreak was linked to the fairground's water system, which supplied food vendors. Later that year, five children became ill with E. coli infections after attending a Carnival of Horrors event at the same fairgrounds.
